Just as the proliferation of automobiles replaced horse-drawn carts and carriages in the urban centers of the world during the last century, so too is AV technology anticipated to replace human-operated vehicles in this century. The earliest traffic issues that arose as automobiles began to flourish were addressed by new authorities having jurisdiction over traffic operations. These new authorities took responsibility to install roadside infrastructure (stop and yield control) to safely manage both the movement of all vehicles and the interaction of vehicles and horse-drawn modes during the transition. Such authorities evolved into the modern automotive age to assess policy and practice to ensure safe operations to mitigate the risk of vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-pedestrian crashes and to install, maintain, and operate modern traffic signaling technology prevalent across our roadway system today. Likewise, our society is at the transportation technology inflection point at which AVs are beginning to operate in mixed traffic with human-operated vehicles as well as pedestrian and other micromobility activity. An OMA (perhaps extensions and/or natural evolutions of existing traffic or transit authorities) is necessary to oversee and manage traffic operations and associated safety concerns when multiple AV fleets begin operating within AMD boundaries. Note that it is not the role of the OMA to operate the AV fleets but rather to regulate their station or curbfront pickup and drop-off locations, facilitate multidirectional communications and data exchange, determine policy, and operate any infrastructure-based systems for signage, sensing, notification, and communications that will ensure the safe passage of all modes. This is similar and analogous to the role of current traffic management with respect to signalized intersection equipment used in modern roadways as well as the communications-based train control systems that have been continuously deployed and improved in automated guideway transit since the 1970s. Ensuring the safety of the traveling public is the primary charge of the OMA. With respect to an AMD, the OMA would focus its safety and hazard analysis not on the internal failures and operational design domain limitations of each AV technology but rather on the operational effect and hazards such failures would have on the traffic and other modal elements within the broader system. Having the OMA develop and enforce appropriate policy for safe operations—as well as plan, deploy, and manage any collective infrastructure within the district—promotes a cooperative and consistent operating environment that allows each AV fleet technology to react predictably and uniformly for a given hazardous condition. This in turn promotes increased safety while minimizing excess congestion that diminishes roadway capacity. Another responsibility of the OMA would be to determine the necessary funding and contracting for the design, procurement, and implementation of any associated infrastructure improvements. These infrastructure improvements may involve simple pavement markings, installation of signage, or erection of appropriate barriers or fencing to control nonvehicular modes from entering the roadway in areas determined to have a high safety risk.
